sources.name: FIDE / Jeff Sonas, 'Sonas Proposal: Repairing the FIDE Standard Elo rating system' (published on fide.com, 20 July 2023)
sources.measures: FIDE Standard (classical) Elo rating of every player on the FIDE rating list, active and inactive, grouped in 100-point bands; January 2023 list (405,074 players) and April 2023 list (approx. 414,000 players)
sources.notes: Published statements: 'the fact remains that 99% of rated players have ratings below 2400 Elo' and 'All players rated below 2000 Elo, which is the bottom 85% of rated players'. January 2023 band counts as published: 1000-1099 23,381; 1100-1199 30,475; 1200-1299 32,444; 1300-1399 33,844; 1400-1499 35,462; 1500-1599 37,324; 1600-1699 38,464; 1700-1799 37,749; 1800-1899 35,851; 1900-1999 31,844; 2000-2099 28,115; 2100-2199 19,818; 2200-2299 11,716; 2300-2399 5,518; 2400+ 3,069 (total 405,074). So 2400+ is about 0.76% of the list and 2300+ about 2.1%; the exact top-1% cutoff sits inside the 2300-2399 band. Pre-dates the March 2024 FIDE compression, which raised all sub-2000 ratings (minimum now 1400) but left ratings of 2000+ unchanged, so the top-1% cutoff is unaffected by it. Document is by FIDE's rating consultant and hosted by FIDE; no mean or SD given.

sources.name: FIDE October 2026 standard rating list, tabulated by JD Chess (research data file elo-2026-10-03.json)
sources.measures: FIDE Standard rating of every player on the October 2026 standard list with a positive published rating and no inactive flag (per-rating counts from the official standard_rating_list_xml.zip, archive dated 2 October 2026, SHA-256 recorded)
sources.notes: Median 1700 is stated in the file. The p99 value is NOT stated: the file gives per-rating counts, from which 2,728 active players are rated 2350 or above and 1,710 are 2400 or above (2300+: 4,136; 2200+: 8,324; 2000+: 27,857). One percent of 221,400 is 2,214, so the top-1% cutoff lies between 2350 and 2400; 2375 is the midpoint of that interval, not a published figure. The accompanying blog page publishes shares at or above thresholds: 2300 = 1.9%, 2400 = 0.8% of active published players. Active-only pool (inactive-flagged players excluded), minimum rating 1400 since the 2024 compression. Third-party tabulation with transparent method; treat as a cross-check on the FIDE/Sonas figure rather than an independent source.

The primary answer uses the FIDE standard (over-the-board classical) list, where FIDE's own 2023 analysis states 99% of rated players are below 2400 and the October 2026 active list places the cutoff between 2350 and 2400 (roughly FIDE Master level). Lurk's set over-represents searched and tracked accounts and gives p99 of 1,522,437 followers; Mention's set is active posting accounts seen by a brand-monitoring tool, and its brackets place the top 1% boundary between 500,000 and 1,000,000 followers. sources.notes: Points read from the sample report's Composite Score Summary: PSI 122 = PR 93, PRI 123 = PR 94, WMI 133 = PR 99, FSIQ 139 = PR 99.5, VCI 145 = PR 99.9, all labelled 'Very Superior' at 130+. sources.name: Triple Nine Society, Qualifying test scores (99.9th percentile)
sources.measures: Minimum scores the society accepts as evidence of the 99.9th percentile: WAIS Full Scale IQ, WISC Full Scale IQ (ages 15 to 16), Stanford-Binet 5 (age 16+), earlier Stanford-Binet forms, Cattell, RAIT.
sources.unit_as_published: IQ points (deviation IQ, mean 100, SD 15 for Wechsler and SB5)
sources.notes: WAIS FSIQ 146; WISC FSIQ 146; SB-5 146; SB Form L/M 151 and SB-IV 149 (SD 16 scales); Cattell IIIB 173 (SD 24); HAWIE-R 146; RAIT 146. WAIS-III not accepted for test dates after 15 February 2015 because of norm ageing. The page itself does not print the percentile; the 99.9th percentile criterion is the society's constitution.

definition: Minimum composite score on supervised intelligence tests that Intertel accepts as evidence of a score at or above the 99th percentile; Wechsler Full Scale IQ (WISC, WAIS, WPPSI), Stanford-Binet 5 IQ, Cattell scales. Stated criterion: 'The only criterion for membership is a score at or above the 99th percentile level on a qualifying and valid supervised test of intelligence.'
caveat: IQ is a norm-referenced score, so the percentile is built into the scale rather than measured in a population survey: Wechsler (WAIS-5, WAIS-IV, WISC-V) and Stanford-Binet 5 composites are scaled to mean 100, SD 15 against a US standardization sample (WAIS-IV n=2,200 adults aged 16 to 90, norms 2008; WAIS-5 n=2,020, norms 2024; WISC-V n=2,200 children, 2014), and 135 is the score those publishers' tables place at the 99th percentile; a Pearson sample report shows 133 already rounding to percentile rank 99 and 139 at 99.5. Percentile ranks are relative to same-age peers in that sample, not to the world population, and the mapping only holds on an SD-15 scale: older Stanford-Binet forms (SD 16) and Cattell scales (SD 24) put the 99th percentile at about 137 and 140 or 156 respectively. Scores on tests with old norms drift upward over time (Flynn effect), so high-IQ societies reject results from superseded editions. The 99th-percentile value comes from society admission thresholds that quote the publishers' norms, not from an independent empirical distribution; a full publisher percentile table is only in the paid technical manuals.

new_metric.definition: Full-scale score on a supervised, individually administered intelligence test such as the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale or Stanford-Binet 5, scaled to a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15 against the test's same-age standardization sample.

sources.name: Brysbaert (2019), How many words do we read per minute? A review and meta-analysis of reading rate, Journal of Memory and Language 109:104047
sources.measures: Mean silent reading rate of healthy adult native speakers aged 17-60 reading normal text for comprehension, pooled across 190 published studies (1901-2019, mostly English, predominantly university students). Unweighted random-effects mean of study-level means. Words counted as published by each study (no character normalisation).
sources.notes: 238 wpm is the unweighted mean across studies (95% CI 230-246); 235 is the MEDIAN OF STUDY MEANS, not a person-level median. SD 51.2 is the between-study SD of study means, not the between-person SD. Weighted subset (87 studies, 10,201 participants, with reported SDs): mean 247.5 wpm, SD 47.4. Mean for fiction 260 wpm, non-fiction 238 wpm. Paper states 'most adults fall in the range of 175-300 wpm' for non-fiction and '200-320 wpm' for fiction; this is a descriptive range, not a stated percentile. Largest single study inside the meta-analysis: Taylor (1965), 12,143 readers grades 1 to college, college students 280 wpm. No percentile table of individual readers is published. Full text read from the author-archived PDF (gwern.net/doc/psychology/linguistics/2019-brysbaert.pdf); data at https://osf.io/3wfas/.

definition: Mean silent reading rate of healthy adult native speakers aged 17-60 reading normal text for comprehension, pooled across 190 published studies (1901-2019, mostly English, predominantly university students). Unweighted random-effects mean of study-level means. Words counted as published by each study (no character normalisation).
caveat: No credible source publishes a 99th percentile (or any percentile) of adult silent reading speed; the best sources give only means, between-study SDs, and descriptive ranges, so a top-1% value cannot be reported without deriving it. Measurement is not standardised: Brysbaert's pooled figure mixes short one-minute tests and hour-long texts, counts 'words' as each study did (English word ~4.6-5.1 letters), and covers native-speaking adults 17-60 who are mostly university students (WEIRD samples), not all adults worldwide. The only person-level SD (260 ± 87 wpm) comes from 48 self-selected highly educated book readers. Bookmate data are Russian-language and truncated above 300 wpm. Comprehension is only loosely controlled; speed without comprehension (skimming, RSVP) can reach 790-1652 wpm in lab tests (Rubin & Turano 1992, n=9) but is a different construct. Rayner et al. 2016 argue rates above roughly 500-750 wpm are not compatible with normal comprehension.

new_metric.label: Silent reading speed
new_metric.definition: Words per minute read silently, with comprehension, when reading ordinary continuous text at one's normal pace.

sources.name: Dhakal, Feit, Kristensson & Oulasvirta (2018), Observations on Typing from 136 Million Keystrokes, CHI 2018
sources.measures: Words per minute on a transcription task of 15 English sentences in an online study hosted with a commercial typing-test site. WPM = (characters in the transcribed string / 5) / minutes from first to last keypress, averaged over sentences. Participants self-selected; 12% excluded for uncorrected error rate above 25% or technical problems. Sample mostly young (mean age 24.5, 75% aged 11-30), 68% from the US, 85% native English speakers, 72% had taken a typing course.
sources.notes: Paper gives mean 51.56 and SD 20.20 for all participants, and defines 'fast typists' as above approx. 78 WPM (faster than 90% of participants) and 'slow typists' as below approx. 26 WPM (slowest 10%). Fast-typist group: mean 89.56, SD 9.53. No p99 is published; the text says the fastest typists reach 120 WPM or more. Distribution described as slightly positively skewed (skewness 0.513, kurtosis -0.11). Data collected over three months in 2016-2017; paper published April 2018. Aalto project page and Cambridge/Aalto news releases repeat these figures and are not independent.

sources.name: TypeLit.io, The State of Typing (updated 16 April 2026)
sources.measures: Per-user average WPM from real typing sessions on TypeLit.io, where users transcribe passages from classic books in 9 languages. Includes users with at least 5 pages typed; users averaging above 150 WPM excluded from most aggregates. Word definition not stated.
sources.notes: Published as threshold shares, not percentiles: 29.9% of users above 60 WPM, 7.3% above 80, 1.3% above 100, 0.1% at 120 or above. The non-standard keys above restate those thresholds as the implied percentile rank (e.g. 100 WPM is exceeded by 1.3% of users). No explicit p99 given. Distribution described as resembling log-normal with a long right tail. Sample is self-selected typing practice users; n stated as '30,000+'.

sources.name: Fastfingers.net, Average Typing Speed & Statistics
sources.measures: Per-test WPM across 7,204,168 timed typing tests on the site (98% are 60-second tests), all languages combined; Indonesian (2.1M tests) and English (2.1M tests) dominate. Scores outside 1-250 WPM excluded. Word definition not stated. Numbers refreshed periodically; no reference date given beyond the 2026 page footer.
sources.notes: Published as bins: 0-19 WPM 15%; 20-39 48%; 40-59 28%; 60-79 8%; 80-99 2%; 100+ 0% (rounded). Page states 10% of tests are 60+ WPM, hence p90 = 60; 2% at 80 or above, hence p98 ≈ 80. English-only average is 33 WPM. Top recorded score 238 WPM. No p99 published; the 100+ bin rounds to 0%, so p99 lies in the 80-99 band on this sample.

definition: Words per minute on a transcription task of 15 English sentences in an online study hosted with a commercial typing-test site. WPM = (characters in the transcribed string / 5) / minutes from first to last keypress, averaged over sentences. Participants self-selected; 12% excluded for uncorrected error rate above 25% or technical problems. Sample mostly young (mean age 24.5, 75% aged 11-30), 68% from the US, 85% native English speakers, 72% had taken a typing course.
caveat: No source publishes an explicit 99th-percentile typing speed. The best academic source (Dhakal et al. 2018, n=168,960) gives mean 51.56 WPM, SD 20.2, and a 90th percentile of about 78 WPM, with the fastest typists at 120+ WPM. Platform data place the top-1% cutoff between roughly 80 WPM (Ratatype, Fastfingers, per-test, large share of beginners and non-English tests) and about 100 WPM (TypeLit, per-user, 1.3% exceed 100). All samples are self-selected online typing-test or typing-practice users, skewed young and towards people interested in typing, not the general population. Per-test and per-user figures differ, test length and error handling vary by site, and the question gives no country, sex or age, so world/all is assumed.
